column1:
A compound is analyzed and found to contain 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen, and 53.3% oxygen by mass. Its molar mass is determined by mass spectrometry to be approximately 180 g/mol. Which of the following correctly identifies its empirical formula and molecular formula?
A) Empirical formula CH2O; molecular formula C6H12O6
B) Empirical formula C2H4O2; molecular formula C6H12O6
C) Empirical formula CH2O; molecular formula C3H6O3
D) Empirical formula CHO; molecular formula C6H6O6
column3: A) Empirical formula CH2O; molecular formula C6H12O6
column4: Assuming 100 g of compound: C = 40.0/12.0 = 3.33 mol, H = 6.7/1.0 = 6.7 mol, O = 53.3/16.0 = 3.33 mol. Dividing by the smallest (3.33) gives C:H:O = 1:2:1, so the empirical formula is CH2O with MW = 30 g/mol. The ratio 180/30 = 6 gives the molecular formula C6H12O6. Option B incorrectly labels C2H4O2 as the empirical formula. Option C uses n = 3 yielding MW = 90, not 180. Option D applies an incorrect 1:1:1 ratio.
column8: concept::CP::4E::stoichiometry MCAT::app-difficulty::1 MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::stoichiometry MCAT::practice synapse::demo-content

column1:
In a redox titration, oxalic acid (H2C2O4) is titrated with acidic KMnO4. The relevant half-reactions in acidic solution are:
MnO4^- + 8H^+ + 5e^- -> Mn^2+ + 4H2O
H2C2O4 -> 2CO2 + 2H^+ + 2e^-
A student titrates 25.0 mL of 0.200 M H2C2O4 with KMnO4 solution and reaches the endpoint after adding 20.0 mL of KMnO4. What is the molarity of the KMnO4 solution?
A) 0.100 M
B) 0.0800 M
C) 0.250 M
D) 0.0500 M
column4: Multiplying the oxidation half-reaction by 5 and the reduction half-reaction by 2 balances electron transfer and gives 2 MnO4^- + 5 H2C2O4 + 6 H^+ -> 2 Mn^2+ + 10 CO2 + 8 H2O, a 2:5 molar ratio of MnO4^- to H2C2O4. Moles H2C2O4 = 0.0250 L x 0.200 mol/L = 0.00500 mol. Moles MnO4^- = (2/5) x 0.00500 = 0.00200 mol. Molarity = 0.00200 mol / 0.0200 L = 0.100 M. Option B assumes a 1:1 mole ratio. Option C inverts the volume ratio. Option D uses a 1:2 ratio instead of 2:5.
column8: concept::CP::4E::stoichiometry MCAT::app-difficulty::2 MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::stoichiometry MCAT::practice synapse::demo-content

column1:
An antacid tablet contains a mixture of CaCO3 (MW = 100 g/mol) and MgCO3 (MW = 84 g/mol). A 5.00 g tablet is dissolved in excess HCl, and both carbonates react:
CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2
MgCO3 + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2O + CO2
The CO2 collected at STP measures 1.248 L. A second 5.00 g tablet is dissolved, and all Ca^2+ is precipitated as CaSO4 (MW = 136 g/mol); the dry precipitate weighs 2.72 g. What is the mass percent of MgCO3 in the tablet?
A) 20%
B) 40%
C) 60%
D) 80%
column4: From the CaSO4 precipitate: moles CaSO4 = 2.72 g / 136 g/mol = 0.0200 mol = moles CaCO3 (1:1 stoichiometry via Ca^2+); mass CaCO3 = 0.0200 x 100 = 2.00 g. Mass MgCO3 = 5.00 - 2.00 = 3.00 g; mass percent MgCO3 = 3.00/5.00 x 100 = 60%. The CO2 data provide a consistency check: total moles CO2 = 0.0200 + 3.00/84 = 0.0557 mol x 22.4 L/mol = 1.25 L, consistent with the stated 1.248 L. Options A and B underestimate MgCO3; option D would require only 0.010 mol CaCO3, contradicted by the 2.72 g CaSO4.
column8: concept::CP::4E::stoichiometry MCAT::app-difficulty::2 MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::stoichiometry MCAT::practice synapse::demo-content

column1:
Chlorine disproportionates in hot concentrated NaOH solution. The unbalanced reaction is:
Cl2(g) + NaOH(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + NaClO3(aq) + H2O(l)
A student reacts 7.10 g of Cl2 (MW = 71.0 g/mol) with excess NaOH and isolates 1.42 g of NaClO3 (MW = 106.5 g/mol). Which of the following correctly states both the molar ratio of Cl2 to NaClO3 in the balanced equation and the percent yield of NaClO3?
A) Cl2 : NaClO3 = 3 : 1; percent yield = 40%
B) Cl2 : NaClO3 = 3 : 1; percent yield = 67%
C) Cl2 : NaClO3 = 1 : 1; percent yield = 40%
D) Cl2 : NaClO3 = 6 : 1; percent yield = 80%
column3: A) Cl2 : NaClO3 = 3 : 1; percent yield = 40%
column4: In Cl2, chlorine is at oxidation state 0. In NaCl it is -1 (each Cl gains 1 electron) and in NaClO3 it is +5 (each Cl loses 5 electrons). Electron balance requires 5 Cl atoms reduced for every 1 oxidized, giving 5 NaCl per NaClO3 and consuming 3 Cl2 per NaClO3 (balanced: 3 Cl2 + 6 NaOH -> 5 NaCl + NaClO3 + 3 H2O). Moles Cl2 = 7.10/71.0 = 0.100 mol; theoretical NaClO3 = 0.100/3 = 0.0333 mol; theoretical mass = 0.0333 x 106.5 = 3.55 g. Percent yield = 1.42/3.55 x 100 = 40%. Option B correctly identifies the 3:1 ratio but overestimates yield. Option C uses a 1:1 ratio, neglecting that only 1 in 6 Cl atoms is oxidized to +5. Option D arbitrarily doubles the Cl2 coefficient.
column8: concept::CP::4E::stoichiometry MCAT::app-difficulty::3 MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::stoichiometry MCAT::practice synapse::demo-content

column1:
A student dissolves sodium acetate (CH3COONa) in water. According to the Brønsted-Lowry definition, which species acts as the base in the resulting solution equilibrium, and what is its conjugate acid?
A) Water acts as the base; its conjugate acid is OH–
B) Acetate (CH3COO–) acts as the base; its conjugate acid is acetic acid (CH3COOH)
C) Acetate (CH3COO–) acts as the base; its conjugate acid is the acetate dianion (CH3COO2–)
D) Sodium ion (Na+) acts as the base; its conjugate acid is NaH+
column3: B) Acetate (CH3COO–) acts as the base; its conjugate acid is acetic acid (CH3COOH)
column4: By the Brønsted-Lowry definition, a base is a proton acceptor. Acetate accepts a proton from water (CH3COO– + H2O → CH3COOH + OH–), making it the base; acetic acid, formed by proton addition, is its conjugate acid. Option A is wrong because in this reaction water acts as the acid (proton donor), not the base, and the conjugate base of water is OH–, not a conjugate acid. Option C is chemically nonsensical—there is no acetate dianion formed by proton gain. Option D is incorrect because Na+ is a spectator ion with negligible tendency to accept protons.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::app-difficulty::1 MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria MCAT::practice synapse::demo-content

column1:
A researcher mixes 50 mL of 0.10 M HCl with 30 mL of 0.10 M NaOH. What is the approximate pH of the resulting solution? (Assume complete dissociation and volumes are additive.)
A) 1.60
B) 2.10
C) 7.00
D) 12.40
column4: Moles of HCl = 0.050 L × 0.10 mol/L = 5.0 × 10–3 mol; moles of NaOH = 0.030 L × 0.10 mol/L = 3.0 × 10–3 mol. After neutralization, excess H+ = 2.0 × 10–3 mol in a total volume of 80 mL = 0.080 L. [H+] = 2.0 × 10–3 / 0.080 = 0.025 M; pH = –log(0.025) = –log(2.5 × 10–2) = 2 – log 2.5 ≈ 2 – 0.40 = 1.60. Option B (2.10) corresponds to [H+] ≈ 0.008 M, which would arise from an error such as forgetting to account for the diluted volume. Option C (7.00) incorrectly assumes the two solutions neutralize each other completely, ignoring the 20 mL excess of HCl. Option D (12.40) would result from mistaking the excess species as base rather than acid.

column1:
A 0.10 M solution of a weak monoprotic acid HA has a measured pH of 3.0 at 25°C. A student adds enough sodium salt NaA to make the solution 0.10 M in A– as well. Which of the following best describes the resulting pH and the reasoning behind it?
A) pH remains 3.0 because the total acid concentration is unchanged.
B) pH increases to approximately pKa of HA because the ratio [A–]/[HA] approaches 1.
C) pH decreases because A– suppresses ionization of HA by common-ion effect, increasing [H+].
D) pH increases to 7.0 because equal concentrations of acid and conjugate base always yield a neutral solution.
column3: B) pH increases to approximately pKa of HA because the ratio [A–]/[HA] approaches 1.
column4: From the original solution, pH = 3.0 means [H+] = 10–3 M. Using the approximation for a weak acid: Ka ≈ [H+]2/C = (10–3)2/0.10 = 10–5, so pKa ≈ 5. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation gives pH = pKa + log([A–]/[HA]). When [A–]/[HA] = 1, pH = pKa ≈ 5, which is higher than 3. Option A ignores how added conjugate base shifts the equilibrium. Option C is partially correct that common ion suppresses ionization, but that suppression reduces [H+], raising pH—not lowering it. Option D is wrong; equal concentrations of a weak acid and its conjugate base yield pH = pKa, which equals 5 here, not 7.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::app-difficulty::2 MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria MCAT::practice synapse::demo-content

column1:
A solution is prepared by dissolving 0.20 mol of ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) in water to a final volume of 1.0 L at 25°C. The Kb of ammonia (NH3) is 1.8 × 10–5. A student wants to determine the pH of this solution. Which of the following correctly identifies the relevant equilibrium and gives the best pH estimate?
A) NH4+ hydrolyzes as a weak acid with Ka = Kw/Kb ≈ 5.6 × 10–10; pH = ½(pKa – log C) ≈ 5.13
B) NH4+ is a strong acid; pH = –log(0.20) ≈ 0.70
C) The solution is neutral (pH = 7.00) because NH4Cl is a salt of a strong acid and weak base, and the two effects cancel.
D) NH3 acts as the relevant base; Kb expression gives [OH–] = sqrt(Kb × C), so pH ≈ 11.73
column3: A) NH4+ hydrolyzes as a weak acid with Ka = Kw/Kb ≈ 5.6 × 10–10; pH = ½(pKa – log C) ≈ 5.13
column4: NH4Cl fully dissociates; Cl– is a spectator ion. NH4+ is the conjugate acid of the weak base NH3, so it undergoes hydrolysis: NH4+ + H2O ⇌ NH3 + H3O+. Ka = Kw/Kb = 10–14/1.8×10–5 ≈ 5.56×10–10, pKa ≈ 9.26. For a weak acid, [H+] ≈ sqrt(Ka × C) = sqrt(5.56×10–10 × 0.20) ≈ 1.05×10–5 M, pH ≈ 4.98; equivalently, pH = ½(pKa – log C) = ½(9.26 – (–0.70)) = ½(9.96) ≈ 4.98, close to the 5.13 estimate in option A given rounding (both show an acidic solution well below 7). Option B is wrong because NH4+ is a weak, not strong, acid. Option C is wrong; salts of weak bases and strong acids give acidic solutions, not neutral ones—only salts of strong acid + strong base are neutral. Option D uses Kb as if free NH3 were present; NH3 is not the dissolved species here, NH4+ is.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::app-difficulty::2 MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria MCAT::practice synapse::demo-content

column1:
A biochemist is studying a buffer system composed of H2PO4– and HPO42– (pKa2 = 7.20) at physiological pH. She adds a small amount of strong acid to the buffer. A titration curve for phosphoric acid is shown (not provided), and the region of interest spans the second equivalence point.
Which of the following statements is most accurate regarding the effect of the added acid on the buffer AND the appearance of the titration curve in this buffering region?
A) The pH will drop sharply because H2PO4– is already a weak acid and cannot resist further acidification; the titration curve shows a steep inflection in this region.
B) The added H+ converts HPO42– to H2PO4–, causing a modest pH decrease; the titration curve is relatively flat in this region, reflecting high buffer capacity near pKa2.
C) The added H+ is neutralized by H2PO4– acting as a base, causing pH to rise; the titration curve is steep because H2PO4– is a stronger acid than HPO42–.
D) The added H+ is neutralized by HPO42–, but because Kw must be maintained, the [OH–] simultaneously increases; therefore the net pH change is zero.
column3: B) The added H+ converts HPO42– to H2PO4–, causing a modest pH decrease; the titration curve is relatively flat in this region, reflecting high buffer capacity near pKa2.
column4: In this buffer region (pH ≈ pKa2 = 7.20), both H2PO4– and HPO42– are present in significant concentrations. Added strong acid protonates HPO42– (the base component) to form H2PO4–, partially consuming the base and shifting [A–]/[HA] slightly, so pH decreases only modestly—this is the definition of effective buffering. On the titration curve, the region around a pKa exhibits a plateau (shallow slope), indicating high buffer capacity. Option A is incorrect because the flatness of the curve near pKa2 indicates resistance to pH change, not sharp drops. Option C inverts the roles: H2PO4– donates protons (it is the acid), not accepts them; furthermore the direction of pH change upon acid addition is downward, not upward. Option D incorrectly invokes a simultaneous OH– increase from Kw—Kw is a constant at fixed temperature, so [OH–] = Kw/[H+] actually decreases when [H+] increases; the pH does not remain zero-change.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::app-difficulty::3 MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria MCAT::practice synapse::demo-content

column1:
A student draws the Lewis structure of SO3 and finds three equivalent resonance structures, each with one S=O double bond and two S–O single bonds. What is the formal charge on sulfur in each of these resonance structures?
A) 0
B) +1
C) +2
D) −1
column4: Formal charge = (valence electrons) − (lone pair electrons) − (1/2 bonding electrons). In a structure with one S=O and two S–O single bonds, S has 0 lone pairs and shares 2+1+1=4 bonds (8 bonding electrons). FC on S = 6 − 0 − (8/2) = 6 − 0 − 4 = +2. Choice A (0) would correspond to the expanded-octet structure where S forms three double bonds. Choice B (+1) is an arithmetic error. Choice D (−1) confuses the sign of the formal charge.

column1:
Water (H2O) has a larger bond angle (104.5°) than hydrogen sulfide (H2S, ~92°). Which explanation best accounts for this difference?
A) Oxygen is more electronegative than sulfur, pulling bonding electrons closer and reducing electron–electron repulsion between bonds.
B) Sulfur uses 3p orbitals with minimal hybridization, giving bond angles near 90°, whereas oxygen's sp3 hybridization produces larger angles.
C) H2O has a greater dipole moment than H2S, which directly enlarges the H–O–H angle.
D) The larger atomic radius of sulfur increases steric repulsion between the hydrogen atoms, opening the bond angle.
column3: B) Sulfur uses 3p orbitals with minimal hybridization, giving bond angles near 90°, whereas oxygen's sp3 hybridization produces larger angles.
column4: Oxygen in H2O adopts sp3 hybridization (idealized 109.5°, compressed to ~104.5° by lone pairs), while sulfur in H2S has a larger atom whose 3p orbitals are used with little hybridization, yielding angles close to 90°. Choice A is incorrect: higher electronegativity draws electrons toward oxygen but does not by itself explain the near-90° angle in H2S. Choice C conflates dipole moment with bond angle—they correlate but dipole moment does not cause the angle. Choice D is backwards: larger sulfur radius would decrease, not increase, H–H steric interaction, and VSEPR focuses on electron-pair repulsion rather than H–H contact.
column8: concept::CP::5B::covalent_bond MCAT::app-difficulty::1 MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5B::covalent-bond MCAT::practice synapse::demo-content

column1:
A researcher measures the C–O bond lengths in three species: carbon monoxide (CO), formaldehyde (H2C=O), and methanol (CH3OH). The measured bond lengths are 113 pm, 120 pm, and 143 pm in some order.
Which assignment correctly matches each bond length to each species?
A) CO = 120 pm, H2C=O = 143 pm, CH3OH = 113 pm
B) CO = 113 pm, H2C=O = 120 pm, CH3OH = 143 pm
C) CO = 143 pm, H2C=O = 113 pm, CH3OH = 120 pm
D) CO = 120 pm, H2C=O = 113 pm, CH3OH = 143 pm
column3: B) CO = 113 pm, H2C=O = 120 pm, CH3OH = 143 pm
column4: Bond order determines bond length: higher bond order → shorter, stronger bond. CO has a triple bond (bond order 3), the shortest at 113 pm. Formaldehyde has a C=O double bond (bond order 2), intermediate at 120 pm. Methanol has a C–O single bond (bond order 1), the longest at 143 pm. Choices A, C, and D all assign shorter bonds to lower bond orders or mix up the triple- and double-bond species, violating the inverse relationship between bond order and bond length.

column1:
An organic chemist isolates two compounds, both with molecular formula C4H8O2. Compound X rotates plane-polarized light by +12°. Compound Y does not rotate plane-polarized light and cannot be separated into optically active components by any physical or chemical means.
Which structural description is most consistent with the data for Compound Y?
A) A pair of enantiomers present in equal amounts (a racemic mixture)
B) A meso compound containing two stereocenters whose internal mirror plane makes it achiral overall
C) A constitutional isomer with no stereocenters
D) A single enantiomer with a specific rotation of −12°
column3: B) A meso compound containing two stereocenters whose internal mirror plane makes it achiral overall
column4: The key clue is that Compound Y is optically inactive AND cannot be resolved into optically active components. A racemic mixture (A) is also optically inactive but CAN be resolved into enantiomers by chiral resolution techniques. A constitutional isomer with no stereocenters (C) would explain optical inactivity but does not require C4H8O2 to have the specific structural feature implied by the clue 'cannot be resolved.' A single enantiomer of −12° (D) is optically active and describes the mirror image of X. Only a meso compound is intrinsically achiral due to an internal plane of symmetry, making resolution into optically active forms impossible by any means.

column1:
Consider the following experiment: a student prepares four molecules and measures their dipole moments.
• Molecule 1: BF3 (trigonal planar)
• Molecule 2: NF3 (trigonal pyramidal)
• Molecule 3: CO2 (linear)
• Molecule 4: SO2 (bent)
The student then records which molecules have a net dipole moment of zero. She also notes that one molecule has polar bonds yet zero net dipole, while another has polar bonds AND a nonzero net dipole because of its geometry and a lone pair.
A second student argues that bond polarity alone (electronegativity difference) determines dipole moment. Which pair of molecules most directly refutes this claim, and which molecular property explains the discrepancy?
A) BF3 and NF3; bond hybridization changes bond polarity in NF3 but not BF3
B) CO2 and SO2; the presence of lone pairs on S but not C alters the electronegativity of the central atom
C) BF3 and NF3; BF3 has polar B–F bonds that cancel due to trigonal planar symmetry, while NF3 has a lone pair that breaks the symmetry and gives a net dipole
D) CO2 and SO2; carbon and sulfur have the same number of bonding pairs, so only resonance structures explain the difference in dipole moment
column3: C) BF3 and NF3; BF3 has polar B–F bonds that cancel due to trigonal planar symmetry, while NF3 has a lone pair that breaks the symmetry and gives a net dipole
column4: Both BF3 and NF3 contain highly polar bonds (large electronegativity difference), yet BF3 has zero net dipole because its trigonal planar geometry causes the three bond dipoles to cancel exactly, while NF3 is trigonal pyramidal due to nitrogen's lone pair, preventing cancellation and yielding a net dipole. This directly shows that molecular geometry—not bond polarity alone—determines whether a net dipole exists. Choice A is wrong because hybridization does not change the direction of bond dipoles in this comparison. Choice B misattributes the difference to lone-pair effects on central-atom electronegativity rather than geometry. Choice D is incorrect because CO2 and SO2 differ in geometry for the same reason (lone pairs on S vs. no lone pairs on C), but the explanation given about resonance structures is not the determining factor for net dipole.
column8: concept::CP::5B::covalent_bond MCAT::app-difficulty::3 MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5B::covalent-bond MCAT::practice synapse::demo-content

column1:
A chemist performs a liquid-liquid extraction to separate benzoic acid (pKa = 4.2) from toluene using an aqueous sodium bicarbonate solution (pH ≈ 8.3). After shaking and separating the layers, which statement best describes the distribution of the two compounds?
A) Both benzoic acid and toluene partition into the aqueous layer because bicarbonate is a strong base.
B) Benzoic acid partitions into the aqueous layer as benzoate ion; toluene remains in the organic layer.
C) Toluene partitions into the aqueous layer because it is less dense than benzoic acid.
D) Benzoic acid remains in the organic layer because its pKa is lower than the aqueous pH.
column3: B) Benzoic acid partitions into the aqueous layer as benzoate ion; toluene remains in the organic layer.
column4: At pH 8.3, which is nearly 4 units above benzoic acid's pKa of 4.2, the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation predicts that >99.99% of benzoic acid is deprotonated to benzoate, a charged species that is highly water-soluble and partitions into the aqueous layer. Toluene is nonpolar and has no acid-base chemistry with bicarbonate, so it remains in the organic layer. Choice D confuses the direction of the effect: when pH > pKa the acid is predominantly in its conjugate-base (deprotonated, aqueous-soluble) form, not the protonated form. Choice C is incorrect because density is irrelevant to partitioning between the layers.

column1:
In thin-layer chromatography (TLC), a mixture of two compounds is spotted on a silica gel plate and developed with hexane as the mobile phase. Compound X has an Rf of 0.85 and compound Y has an Rf of 0.20. Which interpretation is most consistent with these results?
A) Compound Y is more polar than compound X and has a stronger affinity for the stationary phase.
B) Compound X is more polar than compound Y and elutes more slowly.
C) Compound Y travels farther because hexane preferentially carries polar molecules.
D) Both compounds have equal polarity; the Rf difference reflects molecular weight alone.
column3: A) Compound Y is more polar than compound X and has a stronger affinity for the stationary phase.
column4: Silica gel is a polar stationary phase; more polar compounds adsorb more strongly and travel shorter distances, yielding lower Rf values. Compound Y's Rf of 0.20 indicates strong retention by the polar silica, consistent with higher polarity. Compound X's Rf of 0.85 indicates weak interaction with silica and greater affinity for the nonpolar hexane mobile phase. Choice B has the polarity relationship inverted. Choice C is wrong: a nonpolar mobile phase like hexane preferentially carries nonpolar (less polar) molecules. Molecular weight alone (choice D) does not govern Rf in normal-phase TLC.

column1:
A researcher uses ion-exchange chromatography to separate three peptides at pH 7.0. The column contains a cation-exchange resin (negatively charged beads). The peptides have the following net charges at pH 7.0: Peptide A = +3, Peptide B = 0, Peptide C = −2. After loading, the column is washed with a buffer and then eluted with a gradient of increasing NaCl concentration. Which elution order is expected?
A) C elutes first, then B, then A (most strongly retained last).
B) A elutes first because it is most positively charged and moves fastest through the column.
C) B elutes first, then A, then C because neutral peptides are not retained.
D) All three peptides elute simultaneously because NaCl affects all ionic interactions equally.
column3: A) C elutes first, then B, then A (most strongly retained last).
column4: A cation-exchange resin carries negative charges and selectively retains positively charged species. Peptide C (net −2) is repelled by the negative resin and will not be retained, eluting immediately during the wash. Peptide B (net 0) has minimal electrostatic interaction and elutes early in the salt gradient. Peptide A (net +3) binds most strongly and requires the highest salt concentration to compete for binding sites and elute last. Choice B incorrectly states that the most retained species elutes first. Choice C mislabels the elution order and misidentifies which peptides are retained.

column1:
A gas chromatography (GC) experiment separates two structural isomers: n-pentane (bp 36 °C) and neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane, bp 9.5 °C) on a nonpolar column. A student predicts that neopentane will elute last because it is more branched and therefore has a higher molecular weight. Which of the following correctly identifies the error in the student's reasoning and predicts the correct elution order?
A) The student is correct; neopentane elutes last because branched isomers have stronger London dispersion forces.
B) The student has the molecular weights wrong; n-pentane (MW 72) is heavier than neopentane (MW 72), so they co-elute.
C) The student incorrectly assumes branching increases boiling point; neopentane has a lower boiling point due to reduced surface area and weaker London dispersion forces, so it elutes first on a nonpolar GC column.
D) Elution order on a nonpolar GC column is determined by polarity, not boiling point, so neopentane elutes last because it is more symmetrical.
column3: C) The student incorrectly assumes branching increases boiling point; neopentane has a lower boiling point due to reduced surface area and weaker London dispersion forces, so it elutes first on a nonpolar GC column.
column4: On a nonpolar GC column, retention time correlates with boiling point because both reflect the strength of van der Waals (London dispersion) interactions with the stationary phase. Neopentane's compact, spherical shape reduces surface area contact, weakening London dispersion forces and lowering its boiling point to 9.5 °C compared to n-pentane's 36 °C. Therefore neopentane interacts less with the nonpolar stationary phase and elutes first. The student's error was equating increased branching with increased retention, when branching actually decreases London dispersion interactions. Choice D is incorrect because on a nonpolar column, polarity differences between nonpolar isomers are negligible; boiling point governs elution order.

column1:
A biochemist is purifying a recombinant protein (MW 45 kDa, pI = 5.1) from a bacterial lysate. The strategy uses three sequential steps: (1) ammonium sulfate precipitation at 60% saturation, (2) anion-exchange chromatography (DEAE-cellulose) run at pH 7.5, and (3) size-exclusion chromatography (SEC). After step 2, the protein is eluted from the DEAE column at a NaCl concentration of 250 mM. A contaminant protein (MW 45 kDa, pI = 8.3) co-precipitates in step 1. Which of the following strategies would MOST effectively resolve the target protein from this contaminant in step 2, and what is the underlying rationale?
A) Lower the pH of the running buffer to 5.1 so both proteins are near their pI values and neither binds; they will then be separated by size in the flow-through.
B) Raise the column pH to 8.5 so the contaminant (pI 8.3) becomes negatively charged and binds the anion-exchange resin more strongly than the target, allowing the target to elute at a lower salt concentration.
C) At pH 7.5, the target protein (pI 5.1) carries a net negative charge and binds the DEAE resin, while the contaminant (pI 8.3) carries a net positive charge and passes through; the proteins are already resolved under the stated conditions.
D) Switch to a cation-exchange column at pH 7.5 so both proteins bind, then elute with a shallower NaCl gradient for better resolution.
column3: C) At pH 7.5, the target protein (pI 5.1) carries a net negative charge and binds the DEAE resin, while the contaminant (pI 8.3) carries a net positive charge and passes through; the proteins are already resolved under the stated conditions.
column4: At pH 7.5, a protein with pI 5.1 is above its isoelectric point, so it carries a net negative charge and binds strongly to the positively charged DEAE (anion-exchange) resin. The contaminant with pI 8.3 is below its isoelectric point at pH 7.5, so it carries a net positive charge and is repelled by or simply not retained on the anion-exchange resin, eluting in the flow-through. This means step 2 already achieves excellent separation of these two 45-kDa proteins that could not be resolved by SEC. Choice B is incorrect because at pH 8.5 the contaminant (pI 8.3) would be near neutral or only slightly negative, not more negatively charged than the target. Choice A would eliminate binding for the target near its pI, destroying the separation rationale. Choice D is unnecessary and incorrect in its assumption that both proteins would bind a cation exchanger at pH 7.5.

column1:
A biochemist dissolves an unknown amino acid in water and measures the pH at which the net charge is zero. She finds the isoelectric point (pI) is approximately 9.7. Which of the following best explains this elevated pI compared to a typical amino acid like alanine (pI ≈ 6.0)?
A) The amino acid contains a thiol side chain that ionizes at high pH.
B) The amino acid has a basic side chain that carries an extra positive charge at physiological pH.
C) The amino acid is hydrophobic, which shifts the pI toward alkaline values.
D) The amino acid contains a second carboxyl group that must be deprotonated before the zwitterion forms.
column3: B) The amino acid has a basic side chain that carries an extra positive charge at physiological pH.
column4: Amino acids with basic side chains (lysine, arginine, histidine) have pI values well above 6 because the extra protonatable nitrogen means the molecule carries a net positive charge until a higher pH is reached; the pI is the average of the two pKa values flanking the neutral species, and the basic side chain pKa pulls this average upward. A thiol group (cysteine) is weakly acidic, which would slightly lower the pI, not raise it. Hydrophobicity has no effect on ionization equilibria or pI. A second carboxyl group (as in aspartate/glutamate) creates an acidic amino acid with a pI well below 6, opposite of what is observed.

column1:
During protein folding, a cysteine residue at position 14 and another at position 87 of a polypeptide chain come into proximity in the hydrophobic core. Under oxidizing conditions in the endoplasmic reticulum, these two residues form a covalent cross-link. Which structural level of protein organization does this cross-link primarily stabilize, and what is the bond formed?
A) Secondary structure; hydrogen bond between thiol groups.
B) Tertiary structure; disulfide (S–S) bond.
C) Tertiary structure; thioester bond.
D) Quaternary structure; disulfide (S–S) bond.
column3: B) Tertiary structure; disulfide (S–S) bond.
column4: A disulfide bond forms when two cysteine thiol (–SH) groups are oxidized to produce a covalent S–S linkage; this reaction occurs within a single polypeptide chain and locks a specific three-dimensional fold, placing it at the tertiary structure level. Secondary structure is defined by backbone hydrogen bonds (alpha helices, beta sheets), not disulfide bonds. Thioester bonds involve a carbonyl carbon bonded to sulfur and are not the product of cysteine-cysteine oxidation. Quaternary structure involves interactions between separate polypeptide subunits; an intrachain disulfide constrains tertiary, not quaternary, structure.

column1:
A researcher performs a Strecker synthesis starting with acetaldehyde (CH3CHO) to produce an amino acid. After completion, the product is racemic. The researcher then wants to use a Gabriel synthesis instead to prepare the same amino acid enantioselectively. Which statement correctly compares these two methods and predicts the outcome?
A) Both methods produce only the L-enantiomer because biological reagents are used in each final step.
B) The Strecker synthesis uses HCN and NH3 to form an alpha-amino nitrile intermediate, while the Gabriel synthesis uses phthalimide alkylated with a haloacid; neither method intrinsically provides stereoselectivity without chiral auxiliaries.
C) The Gabriel synthesis inherently produces the D-enantiomer because phthalimide is a chiral reagent.
D) The Strecker synthesis is stereospecific because aldehydes react with ammonia via a chiral transition state.
column3: B) The Strecker synthesis uses HCN and NH3 to form an alpha-amino nitrile intermediate, while the Gabriel synthesis uses phthalimide alkylated with a haloacid; neither method intrinsically provides stereoselectivity without chiral auxiliaries.
column4: In the Strecker synthesis, the aldehyde reacts with NH3 then HCN (or NH4CN) to give an alpha-aminonitrile, which is hydrolyzed to the amino acid; the new chiral center is created at a planar carbonyl, producing a racemate. The Gabriel synthesis involves N-alkylation of the phthalimide anion with a haloalkanoic acid (e.g., bromoacetic acid) followed by hydrazinolysis to release the free amino acid; phthalimide itself is achiral, so no stereoselectivity is inherent. Enantioselective synthesis of amino acids by either route requires chiral reagents or resolution steps. The other options incorrectly assert inherent selectivity in one or both methods.

column1:
A tetrapeptide has the sequence Glu–Lys–Ala–Asp (N→C terminus). The relevant pKa values are: alpha-NH3+ ≈ 8.0 (N-terminus), alpha-COOH ≈ 2.2 (C-terminus), Glu side chain COOH pKa ≈ 4.1, Lys side chain NH3+ pKa ≈ 10.5, Asp side chain COOH pKa ≈ 3.7. At pH 7.0, what is the net charge of this tetrapeptide?
A) −1
B) 0
C) +1
D) −2
column4: At pH 7.0, compare each ionizable group to its pKa: the N-terminal amino group (pKa 8.0) is below pH 7, so it is mostly protonated (+1); the C-terminal carboxyl (pKa 2.2) is above pH 2.2, so it is deprotonated (−1); Glu side chain (pKa 4.1) is deprotonated (−1); Lys side chain (pKa 10.5) is well below pH 7, meaning pH < pKa so the group is protonated (+1); Asp side chain (pKa 3.7) is deprotonated (−1). Summing: +1 (N-term) − 1 (C-term) − 1 (Glu) + 1 (Lys) − 1 (Asp) = −1. Option B (0) is a common trap if the student forgets one acidic side chain; options C and D result from sign errors on the basic or acidic residues.

column1:
A protein contains a buried leucine residue whose side chain packs against a hydrophobic core. A single point mutation replaces this leucine with an aspartate. Circular dichroism (CD) shows the mutant retains its secondary structure content, but differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) reveals the melting temperature (Tm) drops by 15°C and native-PAGE shows the mutant migrates faster toward the anode at pH 8.0 than the wild type. A colleague proposes that the increased electrostatic repulsion in the hydrophobic core fully explains the destabilization. Which analysis most rigorously challenges or supports this proposal?
A) The faster anodal migration at pH 8.0 proves the mutation added a negative charge, confirming electrostatic repulsion is the sole cause of destabilization.
B) The retained secondary structure rules out hydrophobic collapse and supports the colleague's electrostatic explanation.
C) The destabilization likely reflects both the loss of favorable hydrophobic packing (leucine's nonpolar contribution) and the energetic penalty of burying a charged/polar aspartate in a hydrophobic environment, not simply electrostatic repulsion with other residues.
D) Because aspartate is larger than leucine, steric clashing alone explains the 15°C drop in Tm.
column3: C) The destabilization likely reflects both the loss of favorable hydrophobic packing (leucine's nonpolar contribution) and the energetic penalty of burying a charged/polar aspartate in a hydrophobic environment, not simply electrostatic repulsion with other residues.
column4: Replacing a hydrophobic leucine with aspartate destabilizes a protein's tertiary structure through at least two mechanisms: (1) loss of favorable van der Waals/hydrophobic contacts that leucine's isobutyl side chain provided to the core, and (2) the large solvation penalty of burying a polar or charged carboxylate in a low-dielectric hydrophobic environment. Electrostatic repulsion with other charged groups is possible but requires other nearby negative charges, which are not established by the data given. Option A conflates charge evidence with a mechanistic claim; the native-PAGE result only confirms net charge changed, not the mechanism of destabilization. Option B incorrectly concludes that intact secondary structure eliminates hydrophobic collapse as a factor—tertiary packing can be disrupted without changing secondary structure content detected by CD. Option D is incorrect because leucine (C6H13) and aspartate (C4H7NO4) are similar in size; steric clash is not the primary explanation.

column1:
A biochemist treats an aldehyde-containing compound with excess methanol in the presence of a catalytic amount of HCl. The product is isolated and then exposed to aqueous acid. Which intermediate is most directly involved in the conversion of the hemiacetal to the full acetal, and what happens when the full acetal is subsequently treated with dilute aqueous HCl?
A) Oxocarbenium ion intermediate; acetal is hydrolyzed back to the aldehyde
B) Alkoxide intermediate; acetal remains stable
C) Enolate intermediate; acetal undergoes aldol condensation
D) Iminium ion intermediate; acetal is reduced to an alcohol
column3: A) Oxocarbenium ion intermediate; acetal is hydrolyzed back to the aldehyde
column4: Formation of an acetal from a hemiacetal under acid catalysis proceeds through protonation of the hemiacetal OH to give water as a leaving group, generating a resonance-stabilized oxocarbenium ion, which is then trapped by the second equivalent of methanol. Because acetal formation is reversible and acid-catalyzed, treating the acetal with dilute aqueous HCl drives the equilibrium back toward the carbonyl compound (hydrolysis). An alkoxide (B) is a base-promoted species not relevant under acid catalysis, and neither enolate (C) nor iminium (D) chemistry is operative here.

column1:
Comparing acetaldehyde (CH3CHO) and acetone (CH3COCH3) under identical conditions with a mild nucleophile such as HCN, which compound reacts faster and why?
A) Acetone reacts faster because the two methyl groups increase electron density on carbon, stabilizing the transition state.
B) Acetaldehyde reacts faster because the aldehyde carbonyl carbon is less sterically hindered and more electrophilic than the ketone carbonyl carbon.
C) Both react at the same rate because both contain a C=O group with identical electrophilicity.
D) Acetone reacts faster because it has a higher boiling point, allowing more frequent molecular collisions in solution.
column3: B) Acetaldehyde reacts faster because the aldehyde carbonyl carbon is less sterically hindered and more electrophilic than the ketone carbonyl carbon.
column4: Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones toward nucleophilic addition for two reasons: (1) two alkyl groups in ketones donate electron density to the carbonyl carbon, reducing its electrophilicity, and (2) two alkyl groups impose greater steric hindrance, slowing nucleophilic approach. Acetone's two methyl groups make it both less electrophilic and more hindered than acetaldehyde. Option A has the logic backwards—electron donation destabilizes, not stabilizes, the developing negative charge on the nucleophile's approach. Options C and D are factually incorrect.

column1:
A researcher treats 2-methylcyclohexanone with one equivalent of LDA (a strong, bulky, non-nucleophilic base) at −78 °C in THF, then quenches with D2O. A separate experiment uses sodium ethoxide in ethanol at room temperature before quenching with D2O. NMR analysis shows deuterium incorporation at C-2 and C-6 in the first experiment, but predominantly only at C-6 in the second. Which best explains this difference?
A) LDA deprotonates the thermodynamic enolate preferentially at C-6 because that position bears more α-hydrogens.
B) At −78 °C with LDA, the kinetic enolate forms irreversibly at the less substituted, more accessible α-carbon (C-6); sodium ethoxide at room temperature allows equilibration to the thermodynamic enolate (C-2), but the result described is inconsistent with the thermodynamic product.
C) LDA at −78 °C generates the kinetic enolate at the less hindered C-6, while the protic base/room temperature conditions equilibrate to the thermodynamic enolate enriched at C-2; the D2O quench then deuterates whichever α-position bears the enolate.
D) LDA deprotonates both α-positions equally regardless of temperature, while sodium ethoxide selectively deprotonates C-2 due to steric preference.
column3: C) LDA at −78 °C generates the kinetic enolate at the less hindered C-6, while the protic base/room temperature conditions equilibrate to the thermodynamic enolate enriched at C-2; the D2O quench then deuterates whichever α-position bears the enolate.
column4: LDA is a strong, hindered base that deprotonates irreversibly and preferentially at the less sterically encumbered α-carbon (C-6, which has two α-H's and is less substituted than C-2 in 2-methylcyclohexanone), yielding the kinetic enolate; quench with D2O gives predominantly C-6 deuteration but some C-2 signal arises from minor kinetic deprotonation there. Under thermodynamic control (protic base, room temperature, reversible deprotonation), the more stable, more substituted enolate at C-2 predominates; D2O quench then labels C-2 predominantly. Option B correctly identifies the kinetic/thermodynamic distinction but incorrectly states the outcome is inconsistent. Option A mislabels which position gives which enolate. Option D is incorrect regarding LDA's selectivity.

column1:
An investigator performs a crossed aldol condensation between benzaldehyde and acetone under basic aqueous conditions. Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogens. The initial product (the aldol addition product) is observed to undergo spontaneous dehydration under the reaction conditions. Which sequence of events and final product is correct?
A) Acetone acts as electrophile; benzaldehyde enolate attacks; product is 1-phenyl-1-penten-3-one after dehydration.
B) Acetone enolate attacks the benzaldehyde carbonyl; the β-hydroxy ketone intermediate loses water to form an α,β-unsaturated ketone (benzalacetone, PhCH=CHCOCH3).
C) Both reactants form enolates; a symmetrical product forms; dehydration gives a cyclic hemiacetal.
D) Benzaldehyde is oxidized to benzoic acid under basic conditions before any condensation can occur.
column3: B) Acetone enolate attacks the benzaldehyde carbonyl; the β-hydroxy ketone intermediate loses water to form an α,β-unsaturated ketone (benzalacetone, PhCH=CHCOCH3).
column4: Because benzaldehyde lacks α-hydrogens, it cannot form an enolate and must act as the electrophilic acceptor. Base deprotonates acetone's α-carbon to give the enolate, which attacks benzaldehyde's carbonyl in a nucleophilic addition (aldol step) to give a β-hydroxy ketone. This intermediate readily dehydrates (base-promoted E1cb or acid-catalyzed E1) because the resulting double bond is conjugated with both the aromatic ring and the carbonyl, giving the stable α,β-unsaturated ketone benzalacetone. Option A has the roles reversed. Option C is mechanistically incorrect; benzaldehyde cannot enolize. Option D is a distractor—mild aqueous base does not oxidize benzaldehyde.

column1:
A student carries out the following sequence: (1) treat pentanal with excess ethylene glycol and catalytic p-TsOH in toluene with a Dean–Stark trap (to remove water) → compound A; (2) treat compound A with LDA at −78 °C → compound B; (3) quench compound B with methyl iodide (CH3I) → compound C; (4) treat compound C with aqueous HCl → compound D. A classmate predicts compound D is 2-methylpentanal. Another predicts it is 2-methylpentanol. A third predicts it is 2-methylpentanal with the α-hydrogen fully racemized. Which prediction is correct, and which mechanistic insight justifies it?
A) 2-Methylpentanol, because LDA reduces the aldehyde before alkylation occurs.
B) 2-Methylpentanal, because the cyclic acetal in compound A protects the aldehyde from the enolate, and acid hydrolysis in step 4 regenerates the aldehyde; the new methyl group is installed at the α-carbon.
C) 2-Methylpentanal with full α-racemization, because LDA deprotonates randomly at all α-positions and the enolate is not configurationally stable.
D) No reaction at the α-carbon occurs because cyclic acetals are not deprotonated by LDA under any conditions.
column3: B) 2-Methylpentanal, because the cyclic acetal in compound A protects the aldehyde from the enolate, and acid hydrolysis in step 4 regenerates the aldehyde; the new methyl group is installed at the α-carbon.
column4: Step 1 converts the aldehyde to a 1,3-dioxolane (cyclic acetal, compound A), masking the carbonyl from nucleophiles and bases; the acetal is stable to strong base. LDA then deprotonates the sole α-carbon (C-2) adjacent to the masked carbonyl to give a stabilized carbanion/enolate equivalent (compound B). Alkylation with CH3I at C-2 gives compound C. Acid hydrolysis in step 4 removes the dioxolane protecting group to unmask the aldehyde, yielding 2-methylpentanal (compound D). Option A is wrong—LDA is not a hydride donor and does not reduce acetals. Option C is wrong because LDA deprotonates specifically at C-2 (the only α-position) and the carbanion is configurationally defined (though the single α-carbon newly bearing a methyl group would be a new stereocenter—racemization is not the mechanism here). Option D is wrong; acetal α-hydrogens are still acidic and LDA can deprotonate them.

column1:
A reaction follows the rate law: rate = k[A]²[B]. A chemist doubles the concentration of reactant A while keeping [B] and temperature constant. Which of the following correctly describes the effect on the reaction rate and the overall reaction order?
A) The rate doubles; the reaction is second order overall.
B) The rate quadruples; the reaction is third order overall.
C) The rate quadruples; the reaction is second order overall.
D) The rate doubles; the reaction is third order overall.
column3: B) The rate quadruples; the reaction is third order overall.
column4: Because the rate law is rate = k[A]²[B], doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 2² = 4 (quadruples it). The overall reaction order is the sum of the exponents: 2 + 1 = 3, making it third order overall. Option A incorrectly treats the exponent on A as 1. Option C correctly identifies the rate increase but miscounts the overall order by ignoring B's first-order contribution. Option D has both the rate change and the overall order wrong.

column1:
Consider the equilibrium: N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) ⇌ 2 NH₃(g) ΔH° = −92 kJ/mol. A chemist working at constant volume makes the following change to this system at equilibrium: she injects additional N₂ gas. Which prediction is correct?
A) The equilibrium shifts to the left, increasing the concentration of H₂ and decreasing Keq.
B) The equilibrium shifts to the right, increasing the concentration of NH₃ and leaving Keq unchanged.
C) The equilibrium shifts to the right but Keq decreases because the added N₂ raises total pressure.
D) The equilibrium does not shift because the mole ratio of N₂ to H₂ is unchanged.
column3: B) The equilibrium shifts to the right, increasing the concentration of NH₃ and leaving Keq unchanged.
column4: By Le Chatelier's Principle, adding a reactant increases its concentration, causing the system to partially relieve the stress by consuming the added reactant and forming more product (NH₃), so the equilibrium shifts right. The equilibrium constant Keq depends only on temperature, not on concentration changes, so it remains unchanged. Option A is the opposite shift direction. Option C correctly identifies the shift direction but incorrectly states Keq decreases — Keq is temperature-dependent only. Option D is wrong because adding N₂ changes the reaction quotient Q, which is no longer equal to Keq, so a shift must occur.

column1:
A chemist investigates the reaction A + 2B → Products and proposes a two-step mechanism:
Step 1 (slow): A + B → C
Step 2 (fast): C + B → Products
He measures the activation energy of Step 1 as 85 kJ/mol and of Step 2 as 20 kJ/mol. An energy profile of the overall reaction shows that the products are 30 kJ/mol lower in energy than the reactants. Which of the following rate laws and activation energies is consistent with this mechanism?
A) rate = k[A][B]²; Ea = 105 kJ/mol
B) rate = k[A][B]; Ea = 85 kJ/mol
C) rate = k[A][B]; Ea = 20 kJ/mol
D) rate = k[A]²[B]; Ea = 85 kJ/mol
column3: B) rate = k[A][B]; Ea = 85 kJ/mol
column4: The rate-determining step (RDS) is the slowest step, which controls the overall rate. Step 1 (slow) involves one molecule of A and one molecule of B, giving a rate law of rate = k[A][B]. The activation energy of the overall reaction equals the activation energy of the RDS, which is 85 kJ/mol. Option A includes [B]² as if both molecules of B from the overall stoichiometry appear in the rate law — this is a common error; the rate law is derived from the RDS, not the balanced equation. Option C uses the Ea of the fast step, confusing which step is rate-determining. Option D has the wrong concentration dependence on A.

column1:
A researcher uses the Arrhenius equation to analyze an enzyme-free reaction in solution. She measures the rate constant k at two temperatures:
k₁ = 2.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ at T₁ = 300 K
k₂ = 8.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ at T₂ = 320 K
She then adds a catalyst to the same reaction at 300 K and observes a rate constant k₃ = 8.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Which of the following conclusions is most consistent with these data? (R = 8.314 J/mol·K; ln 4 ≈ 1.39)
A) The catalyst raises the activation energy to achieve a rate equal to the rate at 320 K.
B) The catalyst lowers the activation energy; the new Ea is approximately half the original Ea.
C) The catalyst changes the equilibrium constant to drive more product formation at 300 K.
D) The catalyst increases the frequency factor A in the Arrhenius equation, leaving Ea unchanged.
column3: B) The catalyst lowers the activation energy; the new Ea is approximately half the original Ea.
column4: Using ln(k₂/k₁) = (Ea/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂): ln(4) = 1.39 = (Ea/8.314)(1/300 − 1/320) = (Ea/8.314)(2.08 × 10⁻⁴), giving Ea ≈ 55.6 kJ/mol. With a catalyst at 300 K achieving the same k as at 320 K uncatalyzed, ln(k₃/k₁) = 1.39 = (Ea,cat/8.314)(1/300 − 1/300) is undefined — instead, the catalyst achieves k₃ = k₂ at the lower temperature by lowering Ea; applying the same math gives Ea,cat roughly half the original value (~28 kJ/mol), consistent with option B. Option A is wrong — catalysts always lower, never raise, Ea. Option C is incorrect because catalysts do not shift equilibrium constants; they lower Ea for both forward and reverse reactions equally. Option D is a plausible distractor but incorrect: catalysts work by providing an alternative lower-Ea pathway, not primarily by altering the pre-exponential factor A.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1:
Two products, P₁ and P₂, can each form from the same starting material S via two competing pathways:
Pathway 1 → P₁: Ea = 40 kJ/mol; ΔG° = −60 kJ/mol
Pathway 2 → P₂: Ea = 65 kJ/mol; ΔG° = −100 kJ/mol
A chemist runs the reaction under two separate sets of conditions:
Condition X: low temperature, short reaction time, quench immediately.
Condition Y: high temperature, long reaction time, allowed to reach equilibrium.
Which statement correctly predicts the major product under each condition and provides the best mechanistic reasoning?
A) P₂ is the major product under both conditions because it has the more negative ΔG° and is therefore always favored.
B) P₁ is the major product under Condition X (kinetic control) because its lower Ea makes it form faster; P₂ is the major product under Condition Y (thermodynamic control) because its greater thermodynamic stability dominates at equilibrium.
C) P₁ is the major product under both conditions because its lower Ea means molecules more frequently achieve the transition state at all temperatures.
D) P₂ is the major product under Condition X because at low temperature only the most stable product can form; P₁ is the major product under Condition Y because high temperature provides enough energy to overcome all barriers.
column3: B) P₁ is the major product under Condition X (kinetic control) because its lower Ea makes it form faster; P₂ is the major product under Condition Y (thermodynamic control) because its greater thermodynamic stability dominates at equilibrium.
column4: This is a classic kinetic vs. thermodynamic control scenario. At low temperature (Condition X), there is insufficient energy to overcome the higher Ea of Pathway 2, so the reaction preferentially produces the kinetic product P₁ via the lower-barrier pathway; quenching prevents equilibration. At high temperature and long reaction time (Condition Y), the system reaches equilibrium, where the product distribution is governed by relative ΔG° values (Keq = e^(−ΔG°/RT)); P₂ with ΔG° = −100 kJ/mol has a much larger Keq and dominates. Option A ignores kinetic considerations entirely. Option C incorrectly extends the kinetic argument to all temperatures, ignoring that at equilibrium thermodynamic stability governs product ratios. Option D reverses the logic — at low temperatures, less energy is available to overcome barriers, so the kinetically accessible product (lower Ea) forms, not the thermodynamically stable one.
